Top Reasons for Investing in Training As shown in Figure 11, at least half of all respondents reported new technology and ensuring quality in services as two of the top reasons their company trains workers2, and 47% shared that training for a certification or program was also a top reason. These priorities highlight the connection between business performance, product expansion, and workforce development. Figure 11. Top five reasons to train workers Training is not just about compliance or meeting minimum standards; it is also a strategy to reduce callbacks (i.e., ensure quality), improve customer satisfaction, and remain competitive as technologies advance. 2 Differences between responses here and those shown in Table 4 are likely due to the fact that the question from Table 4 was open-ended, while this question asked respondents to choose between options. However, the responses to both questions highlight the importance of new skills, technologies, or certifications as a key motivation for contractors to invest in upskilling their existing workers. 20 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Current Training Methods Contractors reported using a range of methods for training their workers, shown in Figure 12. The diversity of training modes suggests that contractors value flexibility and practicality and that formal training can be integrated into daily operations and adopted to different learning styles. Programs offering blended options may be particularly effective. Figure 12. Training modes Companies use many different approaches to training their workers, suggesting a need for various training support resources that can complement and reinforce on-the-job training. Who Pays for Training Responsibility for training costs varies across firms. Employers (52%) and governments (48%) are the top two groups reported to be paying for training, training resources, or exam fees, as shown in Figure 13. Figure 13. Concerningly, at least 30% of contractors reported that workers had paid for training, training resources, or exam fees in the last 12 months. These patterns matter for program design: When workers are expected to pay out of pocket, they may be less able to participate in training, even if they are motivated. Financial support for training—whether through employers, employees, or both—can help reduce these barriers and encourage broader participation. Preferred Training Methods – If Receiving Training Subsidy When asked how they would prefer to train workers if financial support was available, more than 37% of contractors favored hands-on, practical training formats (i.e., on-the-job training), as shown in Figure 14.
